content.title: About
content.content: Fried white fish is a dish made from a blend of several white fish species (such as cod, pollock, hake) that are deep‑fried in vegetable oil until golden and crisp. The fish has a mild, slightly salty flavor, a crunchy exterior, and remains juicy inside.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: A mix of white fish is often used in the food industry to ensure consistent taste and texture.
High‑heat frying retains most of the protein but can reduce the amount of omega‑3 fatty acids.
White fish is a good source of B‑vitamins, especially B12, which supports the nervous system.
Traditionally, fried fish is served with lemon wedges and tartar sauce.
In many countries, fried white fish is a popular street‑food offering.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Fried fish provides high‑quality protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: It contains vitamin B12, niacin, and riboflavin, which support energy metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Fish supplies selenium, phosphorus, and potassium, important for heart and bone health.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: When consumed in moderation, fried white fish has less saturated fat than many red meats.

items.title: Immune support
items.content: Vitamin D present in fish helps strengthen the immune system.

items.title: Fish allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions ranging from skin rashes to anaphylaxis.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Added salt or sauces can raise sodium levels, which is a concern for hypertension.

items.title: Trans fats from frying
items.content: Reusing oil can create trans fats that are detrimental to cardiovascular health.

items.title: Heavy‑metal contamination
items.content: Certain fish species may contain traces of mercury or cadmium; sourcing from reputable suppliers is important.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Fried white fish can be served as a main course with potatoes, rice, or vegetables. It pairs well with lemon juice, fresh herbs, and light sauces. Chopped pieces can be added to salads, tacos, or sandwiches.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep fried fish in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2‑3 days. For longer storage, freeze in a sealed bag for up to 2 months. Reheat to an internal temperature of at least 75 °C before eating.

pasta-with-tomato-based-sauce-seafood-an.title: Pasta with tomato-based sauce, seafood, and added vegetables, ready‑to‑heat

content.title: About
content.content: This is a ready‑to‑eat dish consisting of pasta coated with a tomato‑based sauce, enriched with seafood (shrimp, mussels, squid) and vegetables (bell pepper, zucchini, carrot). The pasta is cooked al dente, the sauce is made from ripe tomatoes, olive oil and aromatic herbs. The product is packaged in a single‑serve pouch designed for quick heating in a microwave or on the stovetop.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The tomato sauce is prepared without artificial colourings or preservatives.
Seafood is sourced from certified sustainable fisheries.
Vegetables are added after the cooking step to preserve maximum vitamins and colour.
Al dente pasta retains a lower glycemic index compared with fully cooked pasta.
The packaging is made from recyclable microwave‑safe plastic.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Seafood and pasta provide high‑quality protein essential for tissue repair and muscle maintenance.

items.title: Lycopene in tomatoes
items.content: Tomatoes contain lycopene, a powerful antioxidant that helps protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Omega‑3 fatty acids
items.content: Seafood, especially mussels and shrimp, supplies omega‑3s that support cardiovascular health.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The pasta and seafood are rich in B1, B2, B6 and B12 vitamins, supporting energy metabolism.

items.title: Fiber and micronutrients
items.content: Added vegetables contribute dietary fiber, vitamin C, potassium and magnesium, aiding digestion and nerve function.

items.title: Seafood allergy
items.content: Individuals allergic to crustaceans or mollusks may experience severe reactions after consuming this product.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: The tomato sauce and seafood can contain added salt; people monitoring sodium intake should consider portion size.

items.title: Gluten
items.content: Wheat‑based pasta contains gluten, making the product unsuitable for those with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Heat treatment
items.content: Heat the dish to an internal temperature of at least 75 °C to ensure any potential pathogens are destroyed.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Place the pouch in the microwave and heat for 2–3 minutes on high power, stirring halfway through. For stovetop preparation, pour the contents into a saucepan, add 30 ml of water and warm over medium heat, stirring until hot.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in a cool, dry place at 2 °C–25 °C. Once opened, keep the remaining product in a sealed container in the refrigerator and consume within 24 hours.

content.title: About
content.content: The sweet frosted roll is a soft sponge cake rolled around a filling and covered with a light sugar glaze. It has an airy texture and a sweet, mildly vanilla flavor highlighted by a crisp sugary coating.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Traditionally the roll is made from several thin layers of sponge cake that are spread with filling and rolled up.
The frosting is usually made from powdered sugar, butter, and a small amount of milk or water.
Sweet rolls are often decorated with sprinkles, nuts, or fresh berries for extra flavor and visual appeal.
In many cultures the roll is served in small portions as part of festive celebrations.

items.title: Energy source
items.content: The carbohydrates in the roll provide quick energy for the body.

items.title: B‑vitamin content
items.content: Sponge cake contains modest amounts of B1, B2, and B6 vitamins that support metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: It provides calcium and iron, which contribute to bone health and blood formation.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: The glaze and cake make the roll calorie‑dense and can raise blood glucose levels.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: Traditional sponge cake uses wheat flour, which may be problematic for people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Fat content
items.content: If butter is added to the frosting, the amount of saturated fat increases.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The roll can be served as a standalone dessert, sliced into bite‑size pieces and paired with berry sauce, ice cream, or fresh fruit. It also makes a convenient sweet snack for on‑the‑go.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the roll in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 2–3 days. For longer keeping, refrigerate it, where it will stay fresh for about a week.

salami-sandwich-on-wheat-with-cheese.title: Salami sandwich on wheat with cheese

content.title: About
content.content: A salami sandwich on wheat with cheese is a popular quick snack consisting of slices of aromatic salami, melted or aged cheese, and fresh wheat bread. The sandwich is often served whole or cut in half, making it convenient for on‑the‑go or office consumption.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Salami originates from Italy, where it is traditionally made from pork, beef and a blend of spices.
Wheat bread provides complex carbohydrates that give a lasting feeling of fullness.
The combination of smoked salami and cheese enhances umami flavor.
Salami sandwiches are a common item on school cafeteria menus in several European countries.
In the US, a popular version adds lettuce and mustard, but the classic version remains without extra vegetables.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Both salami and cheese are good sources of animal protein, essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Source of vitamin B12
items.content: Vitamin B12 found in meat and dairy supports nervous system function and red blood cell formation.

items.title: Calcium from cheese
items.content: Cheese provides calcium, important for bone and tooth health.

items.title: Energy dense
items.content: The mix of carbs from bread and fats from salami and cheese quickly replenishes energy stores.

items.title: Dietary fiber in whole‑grain wheat bread
items.content: When whole‑grain bread is used, it adds fiber that aids normal digestion.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Salami and cheese often contain a lot of salt, which can raise blood pressure if eaten frequently.

items.title: Saturated fats
items.content: A high amount of saturated fat may contribute to elevated cholesterol levels.

items.title: Milk allergy
items.content: People allergic to milk proteins or with lactose intolerance may react to the cheese.

items.title: Preservatives and nitrites
items.content: Some salami varieties use nitrites, which are considered undesirable in excess.

items.title: Gluten in wheat bread
items.content: Individuals with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity should choose a gluten‑free bread alternative.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The sandwich can be eaten cold or lightly toasted. Cut it in half, add mustard, mayo, or lettuce to taste. For a healthier option, use whole‑grain bread and low‑fat cheese.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the assembled sandwich in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 24 hours. Keep salami and cheese in their original packaging separately, and store bread in a dry place to prevent it from drying out.

content.title: About
content.content: Soup is a liquid dish made from broth, water or milk with added meat, fish, vegetables, grains, legumes and spices. Across cultures there are hundreds of variations, from light clear broths to thick creamy soups.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Soup is considered one of the oldest dishes: archaeological evidence shows its preparation over 5,000 years ago.
In Japan popular soups include miso‑soup and ramen, while in Russia you’ll find borscht, shchi and rassolnik.
Soups are often served as the first course of a multi‑course meal because they warm and prepare the stomach for later dishes.
The word “soup” comes from the Latin “suppa”, meaning “to soak up”.
In some countries, such as Poland, a traditional dish called “zupa” is baked in a clay pot, giving a unique texture.

items.title: Rich in vitamins and minerals
items.content: Vegetable‑based soups provide vitamin C, vitamin A, potassium and magnesium, which support immunity and overall health.

items.title: Hydration
items.content: Because soups are mostly liquid, they help maintain proper hydration, especially in colder months.

items.title: Easy to digest
items.content: Warm liquid foods are gentle on the digestive system and the soft ingredients are absorbed quickly.

items.title: Low in calories (when made with the right ingredients)
items.content: Clear broth and vegetable soups often contain few calories, making them suitable for weight management.

items.title: Heart‑friendly
items.content: Soups based on lean meat or fish broth and whole grains can help lower cholesterol levels.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Prepared bouillons and canned soups frequently contain a lot of salt, which may raise blood pressure.

items.title: Allergens
items.content: Soups with dairy, seafood or nuts can trigger allergic reactions in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Bacterial contamination
items.content: Improper storage or reheating can allow pathogenic bacteria to grow.

items.title: Sensitivity to glutamates
items.content: Some ready‑made soups contain added monosodium glutamate, which can cause headaches in susceptible people.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve soup hot, often accompanied by bread, croutons or fresh herbs. It can be prepared in advance and reheated, adding fresh vegetables or protein for variety.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Cool the soup to room temperature, then store it in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze in portions for up to 3 months. Reheat to a rolling boil before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: Soybean curd cheese, also known as tofu cheese, is made by coagulating soy milk with calcium or magnesium salts. It has a smooth, creamy texture, a mild tangy flavor, and is widely used in Asian cuisine as a cheese alternative.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Tofu cheese differs from regular tofu by having a higher protein content and a firmer texture.
In Japan it is called “tofu-no-ko”, while in China it is known as “nǎilào” (奶酪).
It is frequently used in vegetarian and vegan dishes as a substitute for dairy cheese.
Depending on the degree of coagulation, it can be soft or semi‑firm.
Tofu cheese readily absorbs marinades and spices, making it a versatile ingredient.

items.title: Rich in plant protein
items.content: Tofu cheese provides about 15–18 g of protein per 100 g, making it an excellent protein source for vegetarians.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: Unlike dairy cheeses, tofu cheese contains very little saturated fat, which is beneficial for heart health.

items.title: Source of calcium and iron
items.content: Calcium salts used in coagulation boost calcium levels, and soy itself is a good source of iron.

items.title: Contains isoflavones
items.content: Soy isoflavones may support hormonal balance and bone health.

items.title: Low glycemic index
items.content: Tofu cheese has minimal impact on blood sugar, making it suitable for people with diabetes.

items.title: Soy allergy
items.content: Individuals allergic to soy should avoid tofu cheese as it can trigger severe reactions.

items.title: Anti‑nutrient content
items.content: Soy contains phytic acid, which can reduce mineral absorption; heat processing lowers its level.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Some tofu cheeses are brined; people monitoring sodium intake should choose unsalted versions.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Slice tofu cheese for salads, bake it in casseroles, melt it into sauces, add it to sushi rolls, or spread it on toast. Marinating in soy sauce, ginger, and garlic enhances its flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep tofu cheese in its original brine, refrigerated at 0‑4 °C. Once opened, consume within 5‑7 days. It can be frozen, though the texture becomes more crumbly.
